clue.text: Old lecher getting me in the stomach

indicators.note: 'getting me in' says one word goes inside the other, splitting it open

parts.note: gaster is the zoological word for the stomach or abdomen
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dirty old man with something in his belly.
explanation.walkthrough: The stomach is not the everyday word but the zoologist's term for an insect's abdomen; the lecher sense of the answer is archaic, its usual sense being a gambler.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives gamester as an archaic term for a lewd person, a rake, beside its usual sense of gambler.

clue.text: Bulging crone turned up clutching wayward imps

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means read from bottom to top
clutching means holding, so one part wraps around the other

parts.note: a hag is an ugly old woman

indicators.note: wayward means straying from the proper course, so these letters wander out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fat old witch holds on to her naughty little imps.
explanation.definitionFit: Gampish is a dialect word meaning bulging or swelling, like a gamp umbrella when bulkily rolled.

clue.text: I cover up after love in hussy's embrace — it offers new hope for baldies!

definitions.text: it offers new hope for baldies!

indicators.note: 'after' places the following pieces behind the first
an embrace wraps around, so the hussy's word holds the letter for love

parts.note: a minx is a pert or flirtatious girl
love is zero in tennis, O
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lid is a cover

explanation.surface: A flirt's love life is linked with a miracle cure for baldness.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is zero in tennis scoring; in a down clue 'cover up' means the cover is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Minoxidil is a drug first used for blood pressure that was found to stimulate hair growth, sold as a baldness treatment.

clue.text: Former skipper trained tars on American ship

indicators.note: in a down clue 'on' places one piece above, before the next
trained recruits are put into new shape, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
USS stands for United States Ship

explanation.surface: An old ship's captain drilled sailors aboard a US navy vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The skipper is a cricket captain, not a sea captain: Andrew Strauss captained England at cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Strauss captained England's Test cricket team, and skipper is the usual sporting word for a captain.

clue.text: No country-dweller, wet one when it's stormy

indicators.note: a storm tosses things about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A city slicker gets soaked when the weather turns stormy in the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A townee is someone who lives in a town, the opposite of a rustic, often used scornfully.

clue.text: First-born's share of Nuffield estate

indicators.note: a share is a portion taken from inside, so the word is a run of letters within

parts.note: the letters span the two words

explanation.surface: An inheritance dispute over who gets the Nuffield estate.
explanation.walkthrough: Nuffield is the name of a Lord who left a famous foundation, which fits the inheritance picture. The 's is read as 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: The eldest child in a family is the one born first.

clue.text: Carouse is getting stuck into Franconian red

indicators.note: something stuck into another sits inside it

parts.note: rot is German for red, and Franconia is a German region
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker is getting stuck into a bottle of German red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Franconian points to German: Franconia is a wine region of Bavaria, and rot is German for red.
explanation.definitionFit: Roist is an old word for to bluster or revel noisily, related to roister.

clue.text: Soggy bit of bread, hot — one was fresher earlier

parts.note: a sop is a piece of bread soaked in liquid
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: A description of soggy toast followed by a nostalgic remark about student days.
explanation.walkthrough: A soph (short for sophomore) is a second-year student, so a year earlier he was a fresher.
explanation.definitionFit: A sophomore is in his second year at college, so every one of them had been a first-year newcomer the year before.

clue.text: Was looking up after getting round constant low point?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top
getting round means surrounding, so a letter goes inside

parts.note: taken as written
c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
surface padding that also hints the result: saw means was looking

explanation.surface: Someone was looking up after getting round a constant low point in their life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was looking' seems to mean SAW, but 'Was' is taken as written and turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A scaw (or skaw) is a low promontory or headland, a point of land as in the Skaw of Denmark.

clue.text: Showing certain columns I penned, after long lunch in El Vino's?

indicators.note: penned means shut in a pen, so one letter is enclosed by the other word

parts.words: after long lunch in El Vino's
parts.note: plastered means very drunk
taken as written

explanation.surface: A journalist confesses to writing certain newspaper columns after a boozy lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: El Vino's is a Fleet Street wine bar long frequented by journalists, so a long lunch there leaves you drunk; the columns are architectural pilasters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilastered describes a building fitted with pilasters, flat rectangular columns set into a wall.

clue.text: Meat, round end of T-bone, the colour of blood

indicators.note: the meat goes round, so it wraps the selected letter

parts.note: ham is cured pork

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: A butcher's description of a rare T-bone steak, red as blood.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: haem is the pigment in haemoglobin that gives blood its colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Haem is the iron-containing pigment part of haemoglobin, which is what makes blood red.

clue.text: Tropical climbers: one is ariot growing wild round lake

indicators.note: 'round' says the scrambled letters wrap around another word
things growing wild spread out in no set order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: one = A, the indefinite article
taken as written
taken as written
a loch is a Scottish lake

explanation.surface: Jungle vines are running riot as they spread around a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ariot' looks like a typo for 'a riot' but is a real word meaning riotous, used here as plain fodder; 'one' gives A, not I.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristolochia is the birthwort genus, many of whose species are twining vines of warm regions.

clue.text: Archaic slang talk confined to German glossaries

indicators.note: 'confined to' says the word is shut up inside the run of letters that follows

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A note that some old slang word is only found in German word-lists.
explanation.definitionFit: Mang is an old cant verb meaning to speak or talk, used by thieves.

clue.text: Part of entablature with e.g. pictures put up in repository

indicators.note: 'in' places the word inside the other

parts.note: an archive is a store for records

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means turned to read upwards

parts.note: pictures are an example of art

explanation.surface: A gallery hanging pictures on a classical building's frieze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' suggests hanging pictures on a wall; in a down clue it turns the word upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: The architrave is the lowest of the three parts of a classical entablature, the beam resting on the column capitals.

clue.text: Cooking pot — one put in what's fit to eat, removing lid

indicators.note: 'put in' says the word for one is placed inside the other
taking off a lid removes the top, so the first letter goes

parts.note: edible means fit to eat
one = A, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A kitchen instruction about something going into a pot of food with its lid off.
explanation.walkthrough: The lid is the first letter of the word for fit to eat; one gives A, not I.
explanation.definitionFit: A diable is an unglazed earthenware cooking vessel with a wide base and a handle.

clue.text: Secular piece of glass on account of being inserted wrong way round

indicators.note: 'being inserted' says the word goes inside the other one

parts.note: a pane is a sheet of glass in a window

indicators.note: something placed the wrong way round faces backwards, so its letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: 'for' means on account of, as in 'jailed for theft'

explanation.surface: A sheet of glass fitted back to front, described in workman's language.
explanation.definitionFit: Profane can mean secular or not sacred, as in profane music as opposed to sacred music.

clue.text: Extract of yams? Stirred dose in gin

indicators.note: a stirred drink is mixed, so the letters are mixed up too

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy from yams, stirred into gin like a cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: Diosgenin is a steroid compound obtained from wild yams, used to make synthetic hormones.

clue.text: One who earnestly sought rest disturbed with pigeon around

indicators.note: 'with pigeon around' says the bird's name wraps around the jumbled letters

parts.note: quist is a dialect name for the wood pigeon

indicators.note: rest that is disturbed is broken up, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone seeking peace and quiet keeps being woken by a pigeon.
explanation.walkthrough: Quist (also queest or cushat) is a dialect name for the wood pigeon, one most solvers will need Chambers for.
explanation.definitionFit: A questrist is an archaic word, used by Shakespeare, for a seeker, one who goes in quest of something.

clue.text: Gentile girl he excited with kiss

indicators.note: an excited state is a stirred-up one, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young man thrills a non-Jewish girl with a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Shikse (or shiksa) is a Yiddish word for a non-Jewish girl or woman.

clue.text: Keen on opening chart in crow's-nest?

indicators.note: a word opening another splits it open and goes inside

parts.note: a map is a chart
to be into something is to be keen on it

explanation.surface: A sailor in the crow's-nest eagerly unrolling a chart.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a crow's-nest is just one kind of maintop.
explanation.definitionFit: The maintop is the platform at the head of the mainmast, where a lookout's crow's-nest is placed.

clue.text: Tiny amount, or nothing, held in palm

indicators.note: something held in a hand is enclosed by it, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: the ita is the miriti palm of South America
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Something so small it might as well be nothing, held in the palm of a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The palm is a tree here, not the hand; ITA is a crossword regular for a South American palm.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the smallest Greek letter, hence a very small quantity, as in 'not one iota'.

clue.text: Butter potato beginning to dry up, upset about it

indicators.note: 'about' says one word goes around the other

parts.note: ate means upset, as in 'what ate him?'

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: alu (or aloo) is the Indian word for potato

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter
refers back to the reversed potato-and-letter chunk

explanation.surface: Instructions for buttering a potato that has started to dry out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is the verb, to flatter. 'upset' gives ATE, as in 'what's eating you?', and 'it' is the reversed chunk the ATE goes round.
explanation.definitionFit: To butter someone up is to flatter them, and to adulate is to flatter or praise excessively.

clue.text: Leather shroud

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an animal skin used for leather
second meaning: to conceal or cover

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like nouns from a funeral parlour, but the second is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Hide is the noun for an animal's skin made into leather, and the verb meaning to cover or conceal.

clue.text: Jack I exchanged for money for autorickshaw?

indicators.note: one letter exchanged for another is swapped out in place

parts.note: Jack (Jack tar) is a sailor
M is short for money in economics, as in M1

explanation.surface: A sailor swaps cash for a ride in a motorised rickshaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The I in SAILOR is replaced by M.
explanation.definitionFit: A samlor is a Thai three-wheeled taxi, originally pedalled and now often motorised, like an Indian autorickshaw.

clue.text: Was chattering fool catching fish? The opposite

indicators.note: 'catching' would put one word inside the other, and 'The opposite' swaps which one holds which

parts.note: ged is a northern word for the pike
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: Someone talking nonsense about a fool landing a fish, then correcting it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the fool catches the fish, but 'The opposite' reverses the roles: the fish holds the fool. GED is a Scottish and northern name for the pike.
explanation.definitionFit: To gas is informal for chattering idly or at length, so gassed is the past form.

clue.text: Adorned old jar with square inside

indicators.note: 'with square inside' says the letter sits within the other word

parts.note: to grate is to jar, as on the nerves
S is the abbreviation for square

explanation.surface: An antique pot decorated with a square pattern on its inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jar' looks like a pot but is the verb, to grate.
explanation.definitionFit: Graste is Spenser's form of graced, meaning adorned or favoured.

clue.text: Part of fossilized tree — it's vaguely discernible on grand lunar levels

indicators.note: something only vaguely discernible is blurred, so the letters lose their clear order

parts.note: taken as written
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand
maria are the flat dark plains of the moon

explanation.surface: A palaeontologist peering at a faint fossil on the moon's surface.
explanation.walkthrough: The maria (Latin 'seas') are the flat basalt plains on the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmaria is the fossilized root-base of giant clubmoss trees such as Sigillaria, common in coal measures.

clue.text: What serpent shows cutting ultimate bit of sour apple?

indicators.note: cutting the ultimate bit chops off the last letter

parts.note: the serpent of Eden showed malice

explanation.surface: A riddle about the snake in Eden and the apple Eve bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eden serpent and the apple make one scene: malice in, last letter off.
explanation.definitionFit: Malic means relating to apples (Latin malum), as in malic acid, which gives sour apples their sharpness.

clue.text: What only the gullible believe in? Objectively we'll admit owning up

definitions.text: What only the gullible believe in?

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: us is the object form of we

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: of can mean owning, as in 'a man of property'

explanation.surface: A sceptic says we'll own up to the things only the credulous believe in.
explanation.definitionFit: Unidentified flying objects, as alien spacecraft, are a classic thing believed in by the credulous.

clue.text: Old peasant, one remembered for his tunes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an Irish rustic or foot soldier of old
second meaning: the American songwriter Jerome, of Show Boat

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a folk singer; the second half is a famous composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A kern was an Irish lightly armed foot soldier or boor, and Jerome Kern wrote standards like 'Ol' Man River'.

clue.text: Soldier with sword, its head concealed in his cloak

indicators.note: a head that is concealed is not seen, so the first letter drops away

parts.note: a man is a private soldier, as in officers and men
steel is a poetic word for a sword

explanation.surface: A soldier hiding his sword, hilt and all, inside his cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: A manteel is an old word for a cloak or mantle, from French manteau.

clue.text: Crafty old horse a length behind favourite (only third)

indicators.note: 'behind' places one piece after the other
'only third' keeps just a third of the word, its opening portion

parts.note: the first three of its nine letters, one third of the word
an ell is an old measure of length

explanation.surface: Racing commentary: the favourite finished only third, a length behind.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, 'only third' reads as where the favourite finished; here it keeps the first third of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Favell is an old name for a chestnut horse, used as a type of cunning and duplicity, as in 'curry favell'.

clue.text: Classical pianist: you'll find Verdi – – may be varied

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Géza ..., the Hungarian concert pianist

definitions.text: you'll find Verdi – – may be varied
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the two words that fill the gap make a true statement about rearranging letters

explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: put the answer into the gap as two words and 'Verdi and a may be varied' is true, since VERDI with A rearranges into VARIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Géza Anda was a Hungarian-born Swiss pianist celebrated for his Mozart and Bartók recordings.

clue.text: Gynaecological surgeon having nothing against out of control MO's messing with it

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: messing with something throws it into disorder, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: V is short for versus, against
ariot means riotous, running out of control
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A surgeon with no objection while the medical officers make a mess of things.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is a medical officer, which keeps the medical surface going; ARIOT recycles a word from 10 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovariotomy is surgical removal of an ovary, and the surgeon who performs it is an ovariotomist.

clue.text: Overcast? Band of rain we see heading westwards

indicators.note: in an across clue, heading west means running right to left
a band is a strip taken from within, so the word lies inside the following words

parts.note: the letters span the three words

explanation.surface: A weather forecast: overcast skies with rain moving west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overcast' looks like weather but is the sewing term.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcast is to sew over a raw edge with long slanting stitches, so an overcast edge has been sewn.

clue.text: Training cord round front of pastern — does it make horse lame?

indicators.note: 'round' says the cord is wrapped about a letter

parts.note: a creance is a long line used to restrain a hawk in training

indicators.note: 'front of' keeps only the first letter of 'pastern'

parts.note: the opening letter of pastern

explanation.surface: A lunging rope around a horse's pastern, and the worry that it injures the animal.
explanation.walkthrough: A creance is a falconry line, though the surface suggests a horse trainer's rope; the pastern is part of a horse's leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A crepance is a wound on a horse's leg caused by the shoe of the other hind foot, which can lame it.
